newsitem.title: USA: Bristol doubles size with Holiday Inns purchase.
newsitem.headline: Bristol doubles size with Holiday Inns purchase.

text.p: Bristol Hotel Co. said Monday it will acquire 47 Holiday Inn hotels and management contracts for another 14 from British brewing-to-leisure company Bass Plc in a $659 million deal that establishes it as the largest owner-operator of full-service hotels in North America.

The deal more than doubles the size of Dallas-based Bristol, taking its portfolio to 100 hotels and making it the world's largest Holiday Inn franchisee with a total of 84 Holiday Inn, Holiday Inn Select and Crowne Plaza hotels.
In return, Bass will receive 9.37 million Bristol shares, giving it a 36.1 percent stake in Bristol. It will also receive $91 million in cash, and another $300 million in loan repayments.

"This transaction combines the nation's fastest growing owner/operator of full-service hotels with the most widely recognised global brand in the lodging industry," said J. Peter Kline, Bristol's president and chief executive officer.

Founded in 1981 and formerly called the Harvey Hotel Company, Bristol took on its new name shortly before going public last December. It currently operates 39 primarily full-service hotels in seven states with a total of 10,187 rooms, and employs more than 4,500 people nationwide.
Company executives said the acquisition demonstrated that Bristol was focusing squarely on the upper-middle market sector for business travellers.
Kline said a group of banks has committed to advance $505 million in conjunction with the acquisition.

He said Bristol will spend $150 million over the next three years to upgrade the newly-acquired properties, and will convert more of the hotels in its existing portfolio -- which includes Harvey, Harvey Suites and Bristol Suites hotels -- over to Crowne Plaza and Holiday Inn Select flags.

Kline said Bristol has high hopes for the Holiday Inn Select hotels, promising to take on hotel chains like Marriott, Sheraton and Hilton in the lucrative corporate business. "We are going to establish that brand as a major head-on-head competitor with the upscale brands that are competing in the corporate meetings market," he said.
The deal won approval from industry analysts and Bristol's stock gained $1.50 to $30.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"This a tremendous next-step for Bristol and clearly makes their stock much more attractive at this point," said Bill Crow at Southwest Securites Group in Dallas. "It makes these guys a truly national company and elevates their status."

The 61 hotels in the deal have an average occupancy rate of 72.09 percent and an average daily room rate of $73.82. They generated combined operating revenues of $460 million and profits of $69 million for the 12 months ended Sept. 30.

Bass, a leisure group specialising in hospitality, food, drink, and electronic entertainment, plans to hold on to its 36.1 percent stake in Bristol although company executives said their overall strategy was focused on building a global franchise business.
Hotel ownership and management is simply a means of supporting that operation, Bass finance director Richard North said.

Kline said the acquisitions will add slightly to Bristol's earnings in 1997. Following the transaction, Bristol will operate properties in 17 of the top 25 U.S. metropolitan areas. Under the deal, it is acquiring properties in 18 U.S. states and six more hotels in Canada.
About 8,500 Holiday Inn Worldwide employees currently working in the 61 hotels involved in the transaction will become Bristol employees.
